Here's a wild fact to start: when you type the word "unbelievable" into an AI, it probably doesn't see one word — it sees **three pieces**: "un", "believ", "able."

That's because the first thing an LLM does is break your input into **tokens** — not words, not letters, but chunks that the model learned are useful during training.

replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's a fact that surprises most people: an AI language model has never read a single word.

Not one. It has never seen the letter "A" or the word "hello." Everything it processes is numbers — from the very first keystroke you type.

**Tokenization** is how your words become those numbers. When you hit send, your message doesn't arrive as text — it gets sliced into chunks called *tokens*, and each token gets assigned an integer ID. A token is roughly a word or word-fragment: "unbelievable" might split into "un", "believ", "able" — three tokens, three numbers.

GPT-4 works with a vocabulary of about 100,000 possible tokens. Your entire message becomes a list of IDs from that vocabulary before the model touches it.

Here's where it gets interesting: the word "bank" is one token, but it could mean a riverbank or a financial institution. The tokenizer doesn't know which. It just hands the number forward and lets the next stage sort it out.
